pedagogy.summary: This is the representational craft behind correlation: plotting bivariate data as a scatter graph with correctly labelled axes and a sensible, consistent scale, describing the correlation, and drawing an estimated line of best fit BY EYE to read predictions. Three techniques carry it. First, each point represents one subject's pair of values, plotted like a coordinate — the axes must be labelled with the two variables and scaled consistently (a break in an axis is fine when values don't start near zero). Second, the line of best fit is a SINGLE straight trend line following the direction of the correlation, positioned so points are balanced roughly equally either side along its length — not a dot-to-dot join of consecutive points, and not forced through the origin. Third, the line supports INTERPOLATION (estimating within the range of the data, reasonably reliable when correlation is strong) but EXTRAPOLATION beyond the data is unreliable, because the trend may not continue. The characteristic errors are joining the dots, drawing an unbalanced line, and confidently extrapolating past the data.
bestPractices: Plot each subject as one cross using a consistent scale on both axes, labelled with the variables; use an axis break when the data doesn't start near zero rather than distorting the scale
Draw the line of best fit as ONE straight trend line in the direction of the correlation, adjusted so points are distributed as equally as possible either side along its length
Explicitly contrast a line of best fit with a dot-to-dot join — the trend line summarises the whole cloud, it does not connect consecutive points
Use the line to interpolate (estimate within the data range) and flag that estimates are more reliable when the correlation is strong
Treat extrapolation beyond the highest/lowest data values with caution — the trend is not known to continue, so such predictions are unreliable
Keep the representation tied to context so a read-off value is interpreted meaningfully (e.g. predicted score for 5 hours' revision)
keyRepresentations: A scatter of crosses on labelled, consistently-scaled axes (with an axis break where appropriate)
A single straight line of best fit through a point cloud, points balanced either side
The line of best fit contrasted with a wrong dot-to-dot zig-zag
The data range marked on the x-axis, separating the interpolation zone from the extrapolation zone
commonMisconceptions: Joining the points dot-to-dot instead of drawing a single straight trend line
Drawing a line of best fit that is unbalanced (most points on one side) or forcing it through the origin
Extrapolating beyond the data range and treating the prediction as reliable
Plotting on an inconsistent/non-linear scale, leaving axes unlabelled, or swapping the x- and y-values

learn.summary: Learners plot bivariate data as a scatter graph on labelled, consistently-scaled axes, describe the correlation, and, where there is a correlation, draw a single straight line of best fit by eye (balanced with points roughly equal either side, not a dot-to-dot join and not forced through the origin). They use it to estimate within the data range (interpolation) while treating predictions beyond the data (extrapolation) with caution. The discriminating skill is constructing and balancing the line, and knowing where it is safe to read from.

activities.title: Plot and balance a line of best fit
feedback: If points are misplaced, check the scale is even and linear and that x- and y-values have not been swapped before re-plotting a couple of points.
To test balance, count the points above and below the line; if most are on one side, tilt or shift the line until they are roughly equal along its length.
If the learner joins the dots, contrast the zig-zag with the straight line directly: the trend line describes the general direction across all points, the join describes none.
If the line is pinned through the origin or a chosen point, note it does not have to pass through either - reposition it to balance the cloud.
activities.rationale: Plotting and balancing a line is a construction skill that is practised by doing rather than only recognising. A live plotting surface (placing crosses from a table, a scale helper offering an axis break, a draggable line with a running tally of points above vs below) can make the balance concept concrete; these interactive aids are optional ways to surface the mechanism, not required.
sourceClaims: A line of best fit is an estimated straight line drawn in the direction of the correlation, positioned so the plotted points are distributed as equally as possible either side along its length (it may pass through some points); it is a single trend line, not a join of consecutive points, and there is a small range of acceptable answers
KS3 pupils plot bivariate data on scatter graphs with labelled axes and appropriate scales and draw an estimated line of best fit where appropriate
learnerActions: Take a table of paired measurements (e.g. 10 pupils' height and arm-span) and plot each pair as one cross on a two-axis grid.
Label both axes with the variable names and choose a consistent, linear scale; where the data does not start near zero, use an axis break rather than distorting the scale.

First judge the direction of the correlation from the overall pattern (if there is no correlation, do not draw a line). Then draw a SINGLE straight trend line in that direction and adjust it (tilt and shift) until roughly equal numbers of points sit above and below along its whole length.
Deliberately draw a wrong dot-to-dot zig-zag joining consecutive points alongside the correct line, and explain in words why the single trend line, not the join, summarises the whole cloud.
State the correlation type (positive, negative, or none) from the overall pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: The line of best fit is one straight summary of the whole point cloud, positioned so points balance either side - it is not a path connecting consecutive points and is not required to pass through the origin.

activities.title: Interpolate inside, question outside
feedback: If the learner reads a far-outside value confidently, ask: the data only reaches 8 hours - do we actually know the pattern holds at 20? Mark where the data ends.
Reinforce that reliability depends on staying inside the data range and on how strong the correlation is, not on how neatly the line extends.
If the learner thinks extrapolation is simply impossible, clarify it can be attempted but its result is unreliable and must be flagged as such.
activities.rationale: Prediction around and beyond fitted data is a documented source of difficulty, so separating an interpolation zone from an extrapolation zone and voicing the uncertainty targets a real misconception. A shaded data-range band and a prediction marker that turns dashed with an 'unreliable - trend may not continue' warning outside the range are optional ways to make this visible.
sourceClaims: Using the line of best fit to estimate within the range of the data is interpolation (more reliable when correlation is strong); extending the line beyond the data is extrapolation, and since it is unknown whether the trend continues, extrapolated values are unreliable and should be treated with caution

Interpretation errors around prediction from a fitted line are documented — e.g. some students consider that extrapolation is impossible — indicating prediction beyond/around the data is a genuine source of difficulty
learnerActions: On a scatter with a correct line of best fit, mark the data range on the x-axis (the lowest to highest observed value).
Read off an estimated y-value for an x inside the range (e.g. predicted score for 5 hours' revision when the data runs 1-8 hours), and state it as a reasonable estimate.
Attempt a prediction well beyond the data (e.g. 20 hours) and explain why that value is unreliable because the trend is not known to continue.
Note that interpolated estimates are more trustworthy when the correlation is strong, and keep every read-off tied to its context so the number means something.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating within the observed data range is reasonable (especially with a strong correlation), but extending the line beyond the data gives an unreliable prediction because the trend may not continue.

activities.title: Check reading and choice (scorable practice)
feedback: For a wrong line choice, point to how the points distribute either side of each candidate and which one balances.
For a reliability item, reward noting that the prediction lies outside the data range and the trend is unknown there.
For placement, if outside the accepted range, prompt counting points above vs below to rebalance.
activities.rationale: Recognition and read-off items give a quick scorable check and can catch dot-to-dot and extrapolation errors; because recognition does not itself elicit independent plotting and balancing, pair these items with a full construction task.
sourceClaims: A line of best fit is an estimated straight line drawn in the direction of the correlation, positioned so the plotted points are distributed as equally as possible either side along its length (it may pass through some points); it is a single trend line, not a join of consecutive points, and there is a small range of acceptable answers
learnerActions: Given a scatter with a line already drawn, describe the correlation and read an interpolated value.
Choose the correct line of best fit from options that include a dot-to-dot join, an unbalanced line, and a well-balanced line, and justify the choice.
Decide whether a far-outside prediction is reliable and explain why not.
Place a line of best fit onto a given scatter (accepting a small range of acceptable positions).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to recognise a good line and read inside the range confirms understanding, but it does not by itself demonstrate the ability to construct and balance a line from raw data.

activities.title: Annotated reference scatter
feedback: Use this as a model to compare against your own plot — does your line balance the cloud as the example does?
Refer back here if unsure which region is safe to read from.
activities.rationale: A static annotated scatter is a useful worked reference and can present the correct line and zones, but because the example is fixed the learner cannot plot points or balance a line on it — the construction skill must be practised separately.
learnerActions: Study a worked scatter whose axes, correlation type, balanced line of best fit, and interpolation vs extrapolation zones are labelled.
Reveal and read each annotation: what each axis shows, why the line balances the cloud, and where reliable reading ends.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled example clarifies the vocabulary and the target of a good line, serving as a reference before the learner constructs their own.

constraints: The construction step (plotting from a table and drawing a balanced line by eye) is the discriminator; recognition or read-off tasks alone do not show a learner can build a sound scatter, so include an actual plotting-and-drawing task.
An annotated reference scatter is a scaffold: being fixed, it cannot verify independent plotting or line balancing, though it can present correct vocabulary and the target line.
Axis scales must be consistent and linear; an axis break is acceptable when values do not start near zero, but the scale must not be distorted.

Where there is a correlation, the line of best fit must be a single straight trend line in the direction of the correlation with points balanced either side; it need not pass through the origin and must not be a dot-to-dot join. If there is no correlation, no line of best fit should be drawn.

Interpolation within the data range is reasonable (more so with strong correlation); extrapolation beyond the data is unreliable and must be flagged — it is not that extrapolation is impossible, but that its result is untrustworthy.
Keep read-off values tied to context so predictions are interpreted meaningfully.
Interactive aids (draggable line, live above/below tally, shaded data-range band, dashed-line warning) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog fit judgements ('a scatter graph is inherently 2D; a third spatial dimension adds nothing' and 'a dialogue cannot verify a child can place points') are retained only as the narrow objective point that recognition/discussion do not by themselves demonstrate independent construction — not as universal claims about what any medium can or cannot teach.

Original reteach for the dot-to-dot misconception referenced a correlation prerequisite (the concept that the line summarises all points); preserved as the teaching move without the internal prerequisite ID.
No arithmetic or force/motion content to audit; the only idealisation is minor (a plotted cross idealises a data pair) and non-problematic.

Activity 3's attached line-of-best-fit source claim supports the content the recognition items check, not the separate objective limit that recognition does not demonstrate construction; that limit is carried as insight/constraint and is not sourced.

probeDeeper: Counterexample: 'The data only goes up to 8 hours' revision — would you trust the line's prediction for someone who revised 20 hours? Why or why not?' — probes extrapolation
'Why draw one straight line rather than joining the points up?' — forces the meaning of the line of best fit into words
'How do you decide exactly where to draw the line?' — elicits the balance-the-points rule
'Your scale goes 0, 2, 5, 10 — does that matter for where the points land?' — checks understanding of a consistent scale
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: names the correlation (e.g. positive) and reads a value from the line WITHIN the data range (interpolation at 5 hours). Construction: plots each pair accurately on axes labelled with the two variables and a consistent scale (an axis break is acceptable), then draws a SINGLE straight trend line in the direction of the correlation with points balanced roughly equally either side — not a dot-to-dot join and not forced through the origin. Drawing one balanced straight line, and reading only within the data range, are the discriminating moves.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dot-to-dot: joins consecutive points with line segments instead of drawing a single straight trend line summarising the whole cloud
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach what the line represents via the correlation prerequisite: the line of best fit is a single straight summary of the trend across ALL points, not a path connecting them; draw one line in the direction of the correlation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On construction the child connects the plotted points into a zig-zag rather than drawing one straight line of best fit

errorPatterns.pattern: Extrapolation treated as reliable: extends the line well beyond the data range and reads off a prediction as if it were dependable
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: estimates within the data range (interpolation) are reasonable, but beyond it the trend is unknown, so extrapolated values are unreliable and should be treated with caution
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked for a value far outside the plotted range (or on the follow-up) the child reads it off the extended line and states it confidently, without noting the trend may not continue

errorPatterns.pattern: Unbalanced / anchored line: draws a single straight line but with most points on one side, or forces it through the origin or a particular point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child count points above and below and adjust the line until they are roughly equal along its length; the concept of a trend line is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child draws one straight line (right idea) but it is poorly positioned — points not balanced either side, or pinned to the origin

errorPatterns.pattern: Plotting/scale slip: uses an inconsistent or non-linear scale, leaves axes unlabelled, or swaps the x- and y-values so points are misplaced
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: fix a consistent scale (with an axis break if needed) and label both axes before plotting; re-plot a couple of points to check; the understanding is intact, only the setup slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points are misplaced because the scale is uneven or the axes are unlabelled/swapped, though the child understands what a scatter is

responseLevels.gap: Joins points dot-to-dot or cannot plot on a consistent scale (unlabelled/uneven axes); cannot describe the correlation
responseLevels.full: Plots bivariate data on labelled, consistently-scaled axes, draws a single balanced line of best fit by eye, and uses it to estimate within the data range while treating extrapolation with caution — transferring to a fresh data set
responseLevels.partial: Plots the points and describes the correlation, and reads a given line of best fit, but draws an unbalanced line or one forced through the origin, or extrapolates beyond the data without caution — can read a scatter but not construct a sound one

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two moves. FIRST, interpret a given representation: 'Here is a scatter graph of hours revised against test score, with a line of best fit already drawn. Describe the correlation, and use the line to estimate the score for someone who revised 5 hours (the data runs from 1 to 8 hours).' THEN, translate/construct: 'Here is a table of 10 pupils' (height, arm-span) measurements. Plot the scatter graph — label the axes and choose a sensible scale — then draw a line of best fit by eye.' Watch the plotting, the scale, and especially how the line is drawn — that construction step is the discriminator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading a given line is fairly mechanical; the CONSTRUCT step exposes the technique. A child who doesn't understand the line of best fit joins the points into a zig-zag or draws an unbalanced line; a child who doesn't grasp reliability confidently extrapolates far past the data. What they DRAW, and where they are willing to read from it, separate a reader of scatters from someone who can build and use one soundly.
